open_obligations: Check that a stochastic oracle with constant advantage over random guessing is an adequate model of human error.
Note the authors themselves leave open oracles that give incorrect answers on some subset of queries.
Check whether the protocol requires the honest prover to run in polynomial time while the dishonest prover is unbounded; the cited passages do not state this.
If the honest prover must be efficient, check whether this requirement changes the class of decidable problems relative to PSPACE.
out.other_title: Debate is a proposal only for natural language; theory assumes error-free judges
out.rationale: Irving et al. note their theory models judges as error-free and agents as unbounded and call for richer models. Brown-Cohen et al.'s Theorem 6.2 gives a debate protocol with cross-examination for any language decidable by a K-Lipschitz probabilistic oracle Turing machine, with completeness 3/5 and soundness 2/5, in which the verifier V samples from the oracle O to check A's proposed distribution. The authors say human judgement is fallible and reward models approximate it from limited samples, so in practical settings the verifier's oracle O is likely to be flawed, and that Theorem 6.2 partially addresses this by making each response of O stochastic and allowing verification of any computation that outputs the correct answer with a constant advantage over random guessing. The cited passages do not say how the provers' running time is bounded, so the link does not cover Irving et al.'s unbounded agents.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate theory can drop the error-free judge of the DEBATE = PSPACE analogy, for K-Lipschitz probabilistic oracle machines whose stochastic oracle the verifier samples

open_obligations: Check whether the K-Lipschitz assumption excludes the chaotic simulations Irving et al. worry about.
Confirm that the protocol handles adversarially chosen noise at each step, the failure mode Irving et al. describe.
Check whether cross-examination is practical for the debaters in question.

Theorem 6.2 decides a language with completeness 3/5 and soundness 2/5; check whether this gives the typical sample from the simulation's outcome that Irving et al. want, and whether the protocol is learnable by practically realizable agents.
out.other_title: Open: debate protocol for stochastic simulation
out.rationale: Irving et al. leave open a natural debate protocol for stochastic simulation: with noise, a misaligned Alice could choose it so that each single step is plausible but the final result has extremely low probability, and fixing the random seed preserves PSPACE equivalence but gives a protocol likely unlearnable by practically realizable agents. Theorem 6.2 of Brown-Cohen et al. gives a protocol for K-Lipschitz probabilistic oracle machines in which A proposes the probability of each next bit and the provers sample it by coin-flipping through cross-examination, with O(K^2) oracle queries, completeness 3/5 and soundness 2/5; the guarantee needs the Lipschitz condition and cross-examination.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate can efficiently verify stochastic computations, for probabilistic oracle machines that are K-Lipschitz at the human-judgement oracle, where Theorem 6.2 delivers non-trivial savings in verifier time and query complexity whenever K = o(sqrt T)

text: Theorem 6.2 states that any language decidable by a K-Lipschitz probabilistic oracle machine in time T with query length l has an (O(K^2 T log T), O(K^2 + l log T), O(K^2))-debate protocol with cross-examination deciding it with completeness 3/5 and soundness 2/5. A proposes the probability of each next bit, the provers sample it by coin-flipping through cross-examination, and if B aborts the verifier samples from the oracle O to check A's proposed distribution; the authors say savings in verifier time and query complexity are non-trivial when K = o(sqrt T), most interestingly K = O(1).
title: Theorem 6.2: stochastic-oracle doubly-efficient debate with cross-examination
